issue: This term is tagged beginner, but the first common mistake leans on the undefined jargon 'REX loop player' and 'REX slices'. A beginner has no way to know what a REX file is, so the bullet's teaching value is lost on the intended audience and adds cognitive load.
suggestion: Briefly gloss the term in-line, e.g. 'Expecting it to work as a full REX loop player (the sliced-loop format from ReCycle), when it does not trigger individual REX slices or time-stretch independently of pitch' — or replace with a plainer misconception such as expecting per-slice loop playback with independent tempo control.

issue: The opening sentence is a verbless fragment and its referent is vague: 'A way to make a sound quieter when you are off to the side of what makes it.' — 'what makes it' is an unclear stand-in for the sound source, and the fragment breaks the full-sentence pattern used in the following sentences.
suggestion: Rewrite as a full sentence with a clear referent, e.g. 'Cone attenuation makes a sound quieter when you are off to the side of the source producing it.'

issue: Missing possessive: 'the clicks and rattles a brass instrument valves make while being played' treats 'a brass instrument valves' as the subject, which is ungrammatical.
suggestion: Change to 'the clicks and rattles a brass instrument's valves make while being played.'

issue: Missing possessive: 'the rattly, knocking sound a brass instrument valves make' treats 'a brass instrument valves' as the subject, which is ungrammatical.
suggestion: Change to 'the rattly, knocking sound a brass instrument's valves make as they move up and down.'

issue: The definition says the strum runs 'across the courses' and related_terms lists 'Course (paired strings),' implying doubled courses. Web-verified via Wikipedia (Balalaika): the standard/traditional prima balalaika, the instrument this brrr-strum technique belongs to, has THREE SINGLE strings (E4-E4-A4); only less-common factory 6-string variants use three double courses. Calling the strings 'courses' is imprecise for the standard instrument a student would encounter.
suggestion: Change 'across the courses' to 'across the strings,' and consider replacing the 'Course (paired strings)' related term (e.g., with 'Balalaika prima' or 'Folk lute'), or note that doubled courses appear only on some 6-string variants.

issue: The definition says the strum spreads 'across the courses' and related_terms lists 'Course (paired strings)', but a standard balalaika has three single strings, not paired courses. This builds a false mental model, letting a learner confuse the balalaika with a 12-string/mandolin-type course instrument.
suggestion: Remove 'Course (paired strings)' from related_terms and change 'across the courses' in the definition to 'across the strings' so the entry does not teach a paired-course structure the balalaika lacks.

issue: The phrase 'brushes the strings quickly back and forth in fast up-and-down strokes and rattles' is redundant ('quickly back and forth' and 'fast up-and-down strokes' say the same thing) and the trailing 'and rattles' parses ambiguously as either a second verb or a second noun object.
suggestion: Rewrite as: '...in which the index finger (or the whole hand) brushes the strings in rapid up-and-down strokes, producing a continuous, tremolo-like, rattling "brrr" across the courses.'

issue: The romanization in the definition ('zou shou yin') does not match the parenthetical in the term header ('zou yin'), so the reader sees two different transliterations for the same thing.
suggestion: Align the two: use the same romanization in the definition as in the term header (e.g., 'The sliding-hand tone of the guqin (zou yin), ...'), or reconcile them so they are consistent.

issue: The 'stretched rubber band that is playing a note, bending the pitch' analogy evokes changing pitch by stretching/tensioning the string, which is the mechanism of a bend, not of a positional slide (which changes the vibrating length). Since a sibling entry (Meend) uses this same rubber-band analogy where it IS accurate, the mismatch can seed the misconception that a slide raises pitch by tension.
suggestion: Swap to a length-based image, e.g. 'like a trombone slide, where moving the slide smoothly changes the pitch without any break between notes,' so the analogy reflects that the finger moves along the string to change its sounding length.

issue: 'Micing a ngoni' uses a nonstandard spelling of the verb; the rest of this packet consistently spells it 'miking'/'Miking'.
suggestion: Change 'Micing a ngoni' to 'Miking a ngoni' for correct, consistent spelling.

issue: The definition attributes 'the wire mizrab worn on the finger' to both '(sitar, sarod)', and plain_english repeats 'on a sitar or sarod it is a metal finger pick called a mizrab.' This is inaccurate for the sarod: only the sitar's mizrab is a wire plectrum worn on the index finger. The sarod is plucked with a separate hand-held plectrum called a java (jawa), not a wire finger pick. Web-verified via Wikipedia 'Sarod': the sarod is 'played by plucking the strings with a triangular plectrum called a java,' made of 'polished coconut shell, ebony, cocobolo wood, horn, cowbone, Delrin or other such materials.'
suggestion: Attribute the wire finger-worn mizrab to the sitar only, and describe the sarod's plectrum as a hand-held java (jawa), e.g. '...the risha (oud, buzuq), the wire mizrab worn on the finger (sitar), or the hand-held java plectrum (sarod)...'. Correct the plain_english the same way rather than calling the sarod's plectrum a metal finger pick called a mizrab.

issue: The definition says undercutting shifts overtones toward 'musical ratios such as the octave and twelfth.' Mallet bars are not tuned to the octave (2:1). Web-verified via euphonics.org (Chris Chafe/Jim Woodhouse acoustics resource, '3.3 Marimbas and xylophones'): well-tuned bars have the second mode tuned to 3:1 (a twelfth, xylophone) or, more commonly, 4:1 (two octaves, marimba/vibraphone); no bars are tuned to a 2:1 octave. The term explicitly names marimba, xylophone, and vibraphone, all of which use the twelfth or double octave.
suggestion: Change 'such as the octave and twelfth' to 'such as the twelfth (xylophone) or the double octave (marimba and vibraphone)' — i.e., 3:1 or 4:1, not the octave.

issue: The noise-source list is ambiguously punctuated: 'mechanical hum, bearing rattle or brush and commutator buzz' can be misread (e.g., 'bearing rattle or brush' as one item), obscuring that these are three distinct sources.
suggestion: Rewrite as: 'mechanical hum, bearing rattle, or brush-and-commutator buzz, plus any radiated electrical interference'.

issue: The closing clause is a garden-path/run-on that stalls the reader: '...sounded by striking the block over its slit and rounder and softer than the sharp crack of a woodblock.' The 'and rounder and softer' loses its connection to the earlier subject, so a learner has to re-parse to see it describes the tone, not the striking.
suggestion: Split the ideas: '...the 'cluck' is their characteristic dry, hollow, mellow, clop-like tone, sounded by striking the block over its slit. It is rounder and softer than the sharp crack of a woodblock.'

issue: The clause after 'sounded by striking the block over its slit and rounder and softer than the sharp crack of a woodblock' is grammatically garbled: it strings a participial phrase ('sounded by striking...') and predicate adjectives ('rounder and softer than...') together with 'and', so 'rounder and softer' has no proper subject and the sentence does not parse cleanly.
suggestion: Split into two clauses, e.g.: '...sounded by striking the block over its slit. The cluck is rounder and softer than the sharp crack of a woodblock.'

issue: The phrase "the high, breathy overtone tones" is redundant, since "overtone" already denotes a tone.
suggestion: Change to "The high, breathy overtones sounded on the fujara ..."

issue: The clause "Overblow uses the blow reed on the exhale; overdraw uses the draw reed on the inhale" misstates which reed sounds and contradicts the definition's own opening clause (that the normally silent OPENING reed sounds in place of the closing reed). Web-verified via overblow.com (overblow.com/?menuid=152) and Wikipedia 'Overblowing': in an overblow (exhale) the blow reed is choked and the DRAW reed sounds; in an overdraw (inhale) the draw reed is choked and the BLOW reed sounds. As written it names the wrong reed for each technique.
suggestion: Rewrite as: "Overblow is played on the exhale (blow), where the draw reed sounds in place of the choked blow reed; overdraw is played on the inhale (draw), where the blow reed sounds in place of the choked draw reed."

issue: The first and third list items make substantively the same point (do not mistake intentional chiff for a fault/flaw), so the third is redundant.
suggestion: Drop or repurpose the third item ("Assuming chiff is always a flaw when it is often a deliberate articulation of the stop.") since the first item ("Confusing intentional voiced chiff with a speech fault or pipe defect.") already covers it; e.g. replace it with a distinct mistake such as "Over-adding chiff during voicing so fast passages sound spitty rather than clear."

issue: This entry overlaps heavily with the sibling terms 'Organ wind noise' and 'Pipe hiss' (which cross-link each other), yet its related_terms omits both, leaving a learner no way to see how these three near-synonymous organ-noise entries differ.
suggestion: Add 'Organ wind noise' and 'Pipe hiss' to related_terms so learners can navigate between the overlapping organ-noise entries and understand the distinctions.

issue: The phrase "the freely, uncontrolled vibrating reed" is grammatically garbled: the adverb "freely" is comma-spliced to the adjective "uncontrolled", so neither cleanly modifies "vibrating reed".
suggestion: Rewrite as "the freely vibrating, uncontrolled reed gives a strong buzzy quality and a narrow dynamic range."

issue: The mistake "Assuming head-locked and listener-relative are the same thing" introduces the term "head-locked," which is never defined in the entry (and is not in related_terms). A learner cannot self-correct a misconception when the contrasting concept is undefined, so the correction is not constructive.
suggestion: Briefly gloss head-locked inside the mistake, e.g. "Assuming head-locked (a source fixed to the screen/front that does not move even when the head turns) and listener-relative are the same thing" so the contrast is meaningful.

issue: This entry describes the Dolby per-object Size control, which the separate 'Object spread' entry explicitly says is the same thing ('in Dolby tools it is the Size control'). Object size neither lists nor references Object spread, so a learner meeting both entries cannot tell they describe one parameter and may treat them as two different controls.
suggestion: Add 'Object spread' to related_terms (and/or note in the definition that this control is also described as object spread / ADM width-height-depth extent) so the knowledge map connects the two synonymous entries.

issue: plain_english says an object can 'be left out of the headphone mix' for the Off setting, but the entry's own definition states Off/Near/Mid/Far control how much perceived distance and space is applied in the binaural render. Off means no binaural distance processing, not exclusion of the object. As written it teaches the misconception that toggling Off mutes/removes the object on headphones.
suggestion: Reword the last clause, e.g. 'each object can be set to sound close, mid, or far, or have no distance/space processing applied (Off)' — describe Off as no binaural distance treatment rather than as being left out of the headphone mix.

issue: The trailing relative clause 'that normal ear-level speakers cannot' ends on an elided verb, leaving the sentence reading as an incomplete thought.
suggestion: Close the clause explicitly, e.g. '...like rain or a helicopter, which normal ear-level speakers cannot reproduce.'

issue: This device is essentially the same class as the separate 'Immersive monitor controller' entry (both provide central monitor level, mute/solo, source/downmix selection and bass management feeding the speaker array), yet neither entry cross-references the other. A learner is likely to conclude they are two distinct products.
suggestion: Add 'Immersive monitor controller' to related_terms and briefly note the relationship (general multichannel framing vs immersive/Atmos-focused framing of the same device class).

issue: 'Overhead speaker' and the separate 'Height speaker' entry describe the same upper-layer/top loudspeaker component, but neither lists the other in related_terms. A learner may believe they are two different speaker types and try to account for both.
suggestion: Add 'Height speaker' to related_terms and note they are the same upper-layer speaker described with ITU 'top' vs Dolby 'height/top' terminology, so the synonymous entries are linked.

issue: The appositive set off by commas ('between its input, the bed and object feeds from the DAW, and its monitored or recorded output') reads like a three-item list governed by 'between', creating a real parse ambiguity.
suggestion: Set the appositive off with parentheses so the 'between X and Y' frame is clear: 'between its input (the bed and object feeds from the DAW) and its monitored or recorded output.'

issue: The long comma-set appositive ('the speakers defined in its room setup such as L, R, C, LFE, side and rear surrounds and the top channels') separates 'the assignment of ... channels' from 'to the physical outputs', making the sentence hard to parse.
suggestion: Wrap the appositive in parentheses: 'The assignment of a renderer's internal output channels (the speakers defined in its room setup, such as L, R, C, LFE, side and rear surrounds, and the top channels) to the physical outputs of the audio interface that feed each monitor.'

issue: The overhead elevation figure is internally inconsistent within the same entry: the definition states 'about +30 to +45 degrees' while scenario_contexts says 'Setting overhead elevation between 30 and 55 degrees per the layout spec.' A learner reading both fields cannot tell which upper bound is correct, which undermines the entry as a study reference.
suggestion: Make the two elevation ranges agree (align the scenario's upper bound with the definition's, or state one consistent range in both). Defer the exact correct value to the technical reviewer, but the numbers within this entry must match.

issue: This entry's definition is functionally identical to 'Room-rendered monitoring' (also in this group): both = rendering the object/bed mix to the physical in-room speaker array versus binaural headphones. Yet neither term cross-references the other, so a learner meeting both will not know whether they are synonyms or a real distinction, and may invent a difference that does not exist.
suggestion: Add 'Room-rendered monitoring' to related_terms and add a short clause in plain_english or purpose_function noting the two names refer to the same practice (in-room / loudspeaker rendering), so learners treat them as synonymous rather than as separate concepts.

issue: 'Decoy Sound' and 'Misdirection Audio' (also in this group) are near-synonyms - a decoy sound is the concrete technique for the misdirection principle - and Misdirection Audio lists Decoy Sound in its related_terms, but Decoy Sound does not link back to Misdirection Audio. This one-way link leaves a learner studying Decoy Sound without the broader concept that frames it, and hides how the two relate.
suggestion: Add 'Misdirection Audio' to Decoy Sound's related_terms so the cross-reference is bidirectional and learners can see the specific technique within its general principle.

issue: First item reads as a garden-path/awkward construction: 'Looping themed ambience and music play through distributed speakers...' The leading participle 'Looping' makes the subject-verb pairing momentarily unclear.
suggestion: Reword to 'Themed ambience and music loop through distributed speakers along a switchback queue to theme the wait.'

issue: Cold archive and deep archive are listed as related terms and their definitions are near-identical (offline tape, low cost, high latency, rarely retrieved), and each entry only distinguishes itself from 'dark' — never from the other. A learner meeting both back-to-back cannot tell cold from deep, the two most easily confused terms in the cluster.
suggestion: Add a mistake clarifying deep vs cold, e.g. 'Treating cold and deep archive as identical; deep archive is the most dormant, longest-latency end of the spectrum (often the innermost copy in a multi-tier strategy), whereas a cold tier is simply rarely-accessed low-cost storage that may still return files sooner.'

issue: This entry (external clock-reference input, word-clock/AES11 DARS, band-following-one-drummer analogy) is near-identical in scope and wording to the separate term 'Converter clock input' in this same group, but the two do not cross-reference each other, so a learner cannot tell whether they are the same input under two names.
suggestion: Add 'Converter clock input' to related_terms (it already lists 'Converter synchronization output') so the two synonymous input terms are explicitly linked in the knowledge map.

issue: This entry's definition ('the processing delay a signal accrues passing through a converter, dominated ... by the group delay of the digital decimation/interpolation FIR filters') is essentially synonymous with the separate term 'Conversion delay' in this same group, yet neither term links to or distinguishes the other, so a learner meeting both is left wondering whether they name different things.
suggestion: Add 'Conversion delay' to related_terms and add one clarifying clause (in plain_english or as a common_mistake) noting the two terms describe the same fixed converter delay, so the knowledge map connects rather than fragments them.

issue: Grammatical error: 'It is how closely a converter numbers match the real level of each sample' is missing the possessive, so the subject 'a converter numbers' reads as a broken noun phrase.
suggestion: Change to 'It is how closely a converter's numbers match the real level of each sample.'

issue: This entry and the separate term 'Latency reporting' (id 99df4481) describe the same mechanism in nearly identical words (both: plugin reports its added latency in samples via the format's latency interface / getLatencySamples so the host applies plugin delay compensation). Neither term links to the other, so a learner meeting both will likely believe they are two distinct concepts.
suggestion: Add 'Latency reporting' to this entry's related_terms so the two synonymous terms cross-reference, signalling to the learner that they name the same reporting mechanism.

issue: This entry and the separate term 'Delay compensation reporting' (id 46d309cf) define essentially the same mechanism (plugin reports its added latency via getLatencySamples so the host can apply plugin delay compensation). Neither cross-links the other, so a learner is likely to treat the two synonymous terms as different features.
suggestion: Add 'Delay compensation reporting' to this entry's related_terms so the pair cross-references and the learner recognises they describe the same latency-reporting mechanism.

issue: The first list item begins with an all-caps inline label, 'UNSAFE: doing heavy work such as memory allocation...', a label used nowhere else in this or neighboring entries, so it reads as a stray/mislabeled fragment inconsistent with the parallel structure of the other items.
suggestion: Remove the 'UNSAFE:' prefix so the item reads 'Doing heavy work such as memory allocation, locking, or file access inside the callback, which can block the audio thread and cause dropouts or glitches during a live show.'

issue: For an intermediate-tagged term, the definition drops several unexplained, higher-level ML concepts in one clause ('residual vector quantizer and adversarial plus reconstruction losses') that plain_english never scaffolds, adding cognitive load without teaching value at this level.
suggestion: Trim the training-internals parenthetical to keep the definition at the intermediate concept level, e.g. end after 'trained jointly ... to compress and reconstruct audio at high perceptual quality and very low bitrates,' and leave the RVQ/loss-function details out (or move them to a note aimed at advanced readers).

issue: 'acappella' is misspelled; the standard English spelling is 'a cappella' (two words), which the related 'Demixing' entry already uses correctly, creating an internal inconsistency.
suggestion: Change 'Creating an instrumental or acappella from a finished stereo master...' to 'Creating an instrumental or a cappella from a finished stereo master...'

issue: The octave-error bullet ends with 'which raw chroma accuracy tolerates but raw pitch accuracy does not,' introducing two undefined evaluation-metric terms (chroma accuracy, raw pitch accuracy) that appear nowhere else in the entry. For an intermediate learner this clause is opaque and spikes cognitive load in what is otherwise a plainly written mistakes list.
suggestion: Trim the metric clause so the bullet keeps its useful point without the jargon, e.g. 'Overlooking octave errors, since an estimate can be correct in pitch class yet reported an octave too high or low.'

issue: The analogy 'a bit like turning speech into text' primes exactly the misconception that this term's own common_mistakes #1 tries to correct ('Confusing codec tokens with text tokens or word embeddings'). A learner reads the plain_english first and encodes the wrong mental model, then meets the correction, creating avoidable confusion.
suggestion: Recast the analogy to stress that these are numeric indices, not words, e.g. 'a neural codec turns each chunk of audio into a short list of numbered codes (like catalog part-numbers), so a computer can store or process it' and drop the speech-to-text comparison.

issue: The closing analogy is awkwardly worded: "It is like summing up a cloud of points by its longest and widest spread." The phrase "summing up ... by its ... spread" reads as a garbled/wrong-word construction and blurs the intended meaning (describing the cloud by its principal directions of spread).
suggestion: Rewrite as: "It is like describing a cloud of points by its longest and widest directions of spread."

issue: The second common_mistake claims that truncating to a lower bit depth without dither 'can also produce sudden full-scale artifacts that risk hearing and speaker damage at high monitoring levels.' This is technically false: quantization/truncation error is bounded by the quantization step size (at most ~1 LSB), so it cannot reach full-scale amplitude. Web-verified via Wikipedia 'Quantization (signal processing)' (error bounded to +/-Delta/2 for rounding and within the step size for truncation; noise power ~Delta^2/12) and ScienceDirect 'Quantisation Error' overview: quantization error magnitude scales with and stays within the LSB step size, never full-scale. The false full-scale/speaker-damage claim would mislead a certification student about both the magnitude of quantization error and a nonexistent safety hazard.
suggestion: Rewrite to reflect the real effect: 'Truncating to a lower bit depth without dither turns low-level quantization error into signal-correlated (harmonic) distortion, which is most audible on quiet passages and fades/tails.' Remove the 'sudden full-scale artifacts that risk hearing and speaker damage' claim entirely, as truncation error is bounded to roughly one LSB and does not create full-scale output.

issue: The entire entry is a placeholder: definition is '(pending)' and plain_english, purpose_function, practical_application, category, related_terms, common_mistakes, and scenario_contexts are all null. There is no content to certify a technician against.
suggestion: Author the full entry. RipX DeepMix (Hit'n'Mix) is an AI stem-separation and audio-editing application that separates a mix into stems (vocals, drums, bass, other/instruments) and provides note-level (DeepRemix/'Rip') editing of the separated audio. Populate all fields consistently with the other source-separation entries (e.g., Moises, MDX-Net) before launch.

issue: The entry is an unpopulated stub: definition reads "(pending)" and plain_english, purpose_function, practical_application, common_mistakes, and scenario_contexts are all null. A learner reaching this term gets nothing to learn from, so it cannot be assessed for difficulty fit or cognitive load.
suggestion: Author the full entry to the same depth and structure as its sibling stem-separation tools (e.g. Moises, MDX-Net): a plain_english definition of RipX DeepMix as Hit'n'Mix's AI stem-separation/rip-to-notes tool, purpose_function, a practical_application scenario, related_terms (Music source separation, Stem separation, MDX-Net, HTDemucs, Melodyne), and common_mistakes mirroring the shared 'separated stems are AI estimates with artifacts/bleed' misconception.

issue: The third list item ('Mislabeled or biased examples that teach the model the wrong patterns') is a bare noun phrase that names a thing rather than an action, breaking parallel structure with the other two items, which are gerund-led actions ('Testing...', 'Using...'). It also reads as a fragment rather than a stated mistake.
suggestion: Rephrase as an action to match the others, e.g. 'Using mislabeled or biased examples that teach the model the wrong patterns'.

issue: The headword is 'One-mix', but the definition and plain_english only ever define and repeat 'one-off' and never connect the two labels, so a learner is left unsure whether the term they are studying is 'one-mix' or 'one-off' and why it is called 'one-mix' at all.
suggestion: Open plain_english by tying the headword to the concept, e.g. 'A one-mix (or one-off) is a single show that isn't part of a tour, so you get just one shot at the mix.' This anchors the term being learned before switching to the 'one-off' shorthand.
